overview: Aggregation in PySpark reduces many rows into summary values using functions like sum, avg, min, max, count, countDistinct, collect_list, and collect_set from pyspark.sql.functions.

Aggregations run either over an entire DataFrame (producing a single summary row via df.agg(...)) or over groups defined by groupBy, and a single agg() call can compute many measures at once with aliases.

Exact distinct counts (countDistinct) are expensive at scale, so PySpark provides approx_count_distinct, a probabilistic HyperLogLog-based alternative that trades a small error for large speed and memory savings.
learningObjectives: Use agg() with the standard aggregate functions on both whole DataFrames and grouped DataFrames.
Compute multiple aggregates in one pass and alias each result column cleanly.
Choose between exact countDistinct and approximate approx_count_distinct, and understand collect_list vs collect_set.
coreConcept.formalDefinition: Aggregation is the application of an aggregate function - a function that maps a set of input rows to a single output value - over a DataFrame or over groups of rows, returning one summary row per group (or one row total for a whole-DataFrame aggregation).
coreConcept.simpleExplanation: Aggregation is like asking summary questions about a spreadsheet: 'What is the total revenue?', 'What is the average order value per region?', 'How many distinct customers do we have?'. Each question collapses many rows into a single answer, and agg() lets you ask several questions at once.
coreConcept.historicalContext: Aggregate functions come from SQL's GROUP BY and aggregate operators. Spark implements them with partial (map-side) aggregation followed by a final (reduce-side) merge to minimize shuffle. approx_count_distinct is based on the HyperLogLog++ algorithm (Google, 2013), which estimates cardinality in fixed memory and was added to Spark SQL to make distinct counts feasible on billions of rows.

whyItMatters.business: Nearly every metric a business tracks - revenue, active users, average basket size, distinct customers - is an aggregation. Correct, fast aggregations are the foundation of dashboards and KPIs.
whyItMatters.engineering: Aggregations are how raw event data becomes summary tables. Knowing which functions partially aggregate, how to compute many measures in one pass, and when to approximate determines pipeline efficiency.
whyItMatters.scalability: sum/avg/count aggregate partially on each partition before shuffling, so they scale well; collect_list/collect_set and exact countDistinct do not reduce as cleanly and can blow up memory at scale.
whyItMatters.cost: Computing ten metrics in one agg() pass is far cheaper than ten separate scans. approx_count_distinct can cut distinct-count cost by orders of magnitude on large data.
whyItMatters.reliability: collect_list on a huge group can OOM an executor; choosing scalable aggregates and approximation keeps jobs from failing as data grows.

coreComponents.name: Aggregate Functions
coreComponents.definition: Functions from pyspark.sql.functions that reduce a column of values to one value: sum, avg, min, max, count, countDistinct, collect_list, collect_set, approx_count_distinct.
coreComponents.purpose: Express the actual summary computation applied to each group or to the whole DataFrame.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Map a set of input values to a scalar (or an array, for collect_list/collect_set).

coreComponents.name: agg() Method
coreComponents.definition: The DataFrame/GroupedData method that applies one or more aggregate expressions and returns a DataFrame of results.
coreComponents.purpose: Compute multiple aggregates in a single pass and assign output column names via alias().
coreComponents.responsibilities: Accepts column expressions or a {col: func} dict; produces one output row per group (or one total row).

coreComponents.name: Aliasing
coreComponents.definition: Renaming each aggregate output column with .alias("name") so results have stable, readable names.
coreComponents.purpose: Avoid auto-generated names like sum(amount) that are awkward to reference downstream.
coreComponents.responsibilities: Attach a clear name to each aggregate expression in the agg() call.

internalWorking: Spark plans aggregates as a HashAggregate (or SortAggregate) with two phases: a partial aggregate on each partition (map-side combine) and a final aggregate after a shuffle.
For sum/avg/count/min/max, each partition first computes its own partial result (e.g. partial sum and count), so only small partial states are shuffled, dramatically cutting network traffic.

countDistinct must track the actual distinct values, so it shuffles the values themselves and is far more expensive; approx_count_distinct instead shuffles compact HyperLogLog sketches that merge cheaply.
collect_list and collect_set accumulate all values (or distinct values) per group into an array; this state is unbounded per group, so a large group can dominate executor memory.
coreConcept.architectureFlow: DataFrame -> (optional groupBy) -> partial aggregate per partition (map-side combine) -> shuffle partial states by group key -> final aggregate merge -> result rows (one per group, or one total)
dataFlowWalkthrough: 1. df.agg(F.sum("amount"), F.countDistinct("customer_id")) is called on the whole DataFrame.
2. Each partition computes a partial sum of amount and a partial set/sketch for the distinct customers it has seen.
3. Partial sums merge trivially; the distinct-count state is shuffled and merged to produce the global distinct count.
4. Spark emits a single result row with two columns: the total amount and the number of distinct customers.
5. If approx_count_distinct were used instead, step 3 would merge tiny HLL sketches, finishing far faster on large data.

keyTerminology.meaning: Computing per-partition partial results before the shuffle so less data crosses the network.
keyTerminology.importance: Makes sum/avg/count scale; functions without it (like collect_list) shuffle far more data.

keyTerminology.meaning: count(col) counts non-null values; countDistinct(col) counts unique values, which requires tracking all distinct values.
keyTerminology.importance: countDistinct is much more expensive because it cannot be reduced to a simple running counter.

keyTerminology.meaning: A HyperLogLog-based estimate of distinct cardinality using fixed memory, with a configurable relative standard deviation (default ~5%).
keyTerminology.importance: Turns an infeasible exact distinct count on billions of rows into a fast, bounded-memory operation.

keyTerminology.meaning: collect_list gathers all values per group into an array (keeps duplicates and is non-deterministic in order); collect_set gathers only distinct values.
keyTerminology.importance: Both build unbounded per-group arrays, so they risk memory blowups on large groups.

importantConcepts.explanation: df.agg(...) with no groupBy returns exactly one summary row over all data. df.groupBy("region").agg(...) returns one row per group. The same aggregate functions work in both cases.
Passing several aggregate expressions to a single agg() call computes them all in one scan/shuffle, which is far cheaper than calling agg() repeatedly or unioning separate results.
sum/avg/min/max ignore nulls; count(col) ignores nulls while count("*") counts all rows including nulls. countDistinct also ignores nulls. Knowing this prevents subtle metric errors.

variationsAndTypes: **Numeric reducers:** sum, avg, min, max - compute partial state per partition and merge cheaply.
**Counters:** count (rows / non-null values), countDistinct (exact unique), approx_count_distinct (estimated unique).
**Collectors:** collect_list (all values, with duplicates) and collect_set (distinct values) build arrays per group.
**Statistical aggregates:** stddev, variance, skewness, kurtosis, and percentile_approx for distribution summaries.
**Conditional aggregates:** combine with when()/filter inside the aggregate, e.g. F.sum(F.when(cond, 1).otherwise(0)).
advantages: **Single-pass efficiency:** many measures computed in one scan and shuffle via agg().
**Scalable reducers:** sum/avg/count/min/max aggregate partially before shuffling, minimizing network cost.
**Approximation option:** approx_count_distinct delivers fast, bounded-memory cardinality on huge data.
**Expressive:** collectors and conditional aggregates capture complex summaries declaratively.
disadvantages: **collect_list/collect_set memory risk:** unbounded per-group arrays can OOM executors on large or skewed groups.
**Exact countDistinct cost:** must shuffle and track all distinct values, expensive at scale.
**Non-determinism:** collect_list order is not guaranteed; results can vary across runs.
**Skew exposure:** a single heavy group concentrates work on one task during the final aggregate.

tradeOffs.whenToUse: Use exact countDistinct when correctness is mandatory and cardinality is modest. Use approx_count_distinct for large-scale dashboards where a few percent error is acceptable. Use collect_set only when group sizes are bounded.
tradeOffs.whenToAvoid: Avoid collect_list/collect_set on unbounded or skewed groups. Avoid many separate agg() calls when one combined call suffices. Avoid exact distinct counts on billions of rows when an estimate is acceptable.

coreConcept.realWorldAnalogy: Aggregation is like a cashier tallying a shopping cart: sum totals the prices, count counts the items, max finds the most expensive item, and countDistinct counts how many different products were bought. collect_list is writing down every item on the receipt; collect_set is listing each unique product once. approx_count_distinct is estimating 'about 50 unique products' from a quick glance instead of counting each one exactly.

commonMisconceptions.myth: countDistinct and approx_count_distinct cost about the same.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Exact countDistinct must track every distinct value and shuffle them, while approx_count_distinct uses fixed-size HyperLogLog sketches; on large data the approximate version is dramatically faster and lighter.

commonMisconceptions.myth: collect_list always returns values in a deterministic order.
commonMisconceptions.reality: collect_list order reflects partition/processing order and is not guaranteed; if order matters you must sort explicitly or use array sorting after collection.

productionConsiderations.scalability: Reducer aggregates scale linearly thanks to map-side combine; collect_list/collect_set and exact countDistinct grow with group cardinality and can dominate memory, so cap group sizes or switch to approximation.
productionConsiderations.reliability: The most common aggregation failure is an executor OOM from collect_list on a giant group; bound group sizes, filter early, and prefer approx functions to keep jobs stable.
productionConsiderations.faultTolerance: Aggregation state is recomputed from lineage on task failure; partial aggregation keeps the shuffle small, which speeds recovery after executor loss.
productionConsiderations.monitoring: Watch the final aggregate stage for skewed tasks (one heavy group) and for spill caused by large collect_list arrays; track output row counts to validate grouping.
productionConsiderations.security: collect_list can gather raw sensitive values into arrays; mask or hash columns before collecting when handling regulated data.
productionConsiderations.costOptimization: Combine measures into one agg() pass, push filters before aggregation, and use approx_count_distinct to cut distinct-count cost by orders of magnitude.
productionConsiderations.performance: Project only needed columns before aggregating, set the relative SD on approx_count_distinct to balance accuracy vs speed, and avoid collecting unbounded arrays you do not need.

codeExamples.title: Whole-DataFrame aggregation with multiple measures and aliases
codeExamples.overview: Computes several aggregates over the entire DataFrame in a single agg() call, naming each output column.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.appName("agg").getOrCreate()

orders = spark.createDataFrame(
    [(1, "US", 250.0), (2, "US", 75.0), (3, "UK", 400.0),
     (4, "UK", 120.0), (5, "US", 250.0)],
    ["customer_id", "region", "amount"],
)

summary = orders.agg(
    F.sum("amount").alias("total_amount"),
    F.avg("amount").alias("avg_amount"),
    F.min("amount").alias("min_amount"),
    F.max("amount").alias("max_amount"),
    F.count("*").alias("num_orders"),
    F.countDistinct("customer_id").alias("unique_customers"),
)
summary.show()
codeExamples.breakdown: With no groupBy, agg() reduces all rows to a single summary row. Each aggregate function is wrapped with .alias() to control the output column name instead of getting auto-names like sum(amount). count("*") counts every row; countDistinct counts unique customer_id values.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: One row: total_amount=1095.0, avg_amount=219.0, min_amount=75.0, max_amount=400.0, num_orders=5, unique_customers=5.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Forgetting .alias() leaves unwieldy column names; using count("col") instead of count("*") silently skips null values; mixing countDistinct with other aggregates is fine but can be slow at scale.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Compute all measures in one agg() call to scan and shuffle once. If unique_customers is on billions of rows and approximate is acceptable, swap countDistinct for approx_count_distinct.

codeExamples.title: Grouped aggregation with collectors and conditional sums
codeExamples.overview: Aggregates per region, building collect_list/collect_set arrays and a conditional count in the same pass.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

by_region = orders.groupBy("region").agg(
    F.sum("amount").alias("region_total"),
    F.avg("amount").alias("region_avg"),
    F.collect_list("amount").alias("all_amounts"),
    F.collect_set("customer_id").alias("distinct_customers"),
    F.countDistinct("customer_id").alias("n_customers"),
    F.sum(F.when(F.col("amount") > 200, 1).otherwise(0)).alias("big_orders"),
)
by_region.orderBy("region").show(truncate=False)
codeExamples.breakdown: groupBy("region") creates one row per region. collect_list gathers every amount (duplicates kept) while collect_set gathers distinct customer_ids. The conditional F.sum(F.when(...)) counts orders above 200 by summing 1s and 0s - a common pattern for conditional aggregation. All measures are computed in one shuffle.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: Two rows. UK: region_total=520.0, all_amounts=[400.0,120.0], big_orders=1. US: region_total=575.0, all_amounts=[250.0,75.0,250.0], distinct_customers={1,2,5}, big_orders=2.
codeExamples.commonIssues: collect_list on a very large group can OOM the executor; collect_list order is non-deterministic; collect_set deduplicates but is still unbounded per group.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use collectors only when group sizes are bounded. If you just need the count of distinct values, use countDistinct/approx_count_distinct instead of collect_set then size().

codeExamples.title: Exact vs approximate distinct count
codeExamples.overview: Compares countDistinct with approx_count_distinct, including tuning the accuracy parameter.
codeExamples.code:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Exact distinct - accurate but shuffles all distinct values
exact = orders.agg(
    F.countDistinct("customer_id").alias("exact_uniques")
)

# Approximate distinct - HyperLogLog, fixed memory, ~5% default error
approx_default = orders.agg(
    F.approx_count_distinct("customer_id").alias("approx_uniques")
)

# Tighter accuracy: rsd = relative standard deviation (smaller = more accurate, more memory)
approx_tight = orders.agg(
    F.approx_count_distinct("customer_id", rsd=0.01).alias("approx_uniques_1pct")
)

exact.show()
approx_default.show()
approx_tight.show()
codeExamples.breakdown: countDistinct returns the exact unique count by tracking all distinct values. approx_count_distinct estimates it with a HyperLogLog sketch in fixed memory; the optional rsd parameter sets the target relative standard deviation (default ~0.05). Lowering rsd to 0.01 increases accuracy at the cost of more memory per sketch.
codeExamples.expectedOutput: On this tiny dataset all three return 3 (customers 1,2,5 plus 3,4 = 5 distinct). On billions of rows the approximate versions run far faster while the exact version may be slow or memory-heavy.
codeExamples.commonIssues: Assuming approx is exact (it has bounded error); setting rsd too low defeats the memory savings; using exact countDistinct on huge data and hitting long runtimes or spill.
codeExamples.optimizationTips: Use approx_count_distinct for large-scale dashboards and reserve countDistinct for cases where exactness is required. Tune rsd only as tight as the business tolerance demands.

endToEndExample.businessProblem: A marketplace needs a daily metrics table per seller: total and average sales, order count, number of distinct buyers, and the set of categories sold, computed over a billion-row order-line table.
endToEndExample.inputData: order_lines (order_id, seller_id, buyer_id, category, amount) ~1 billion rows in Parquet.
endToEndExample.architecture: PySpark on Spark 3.x reading Parquet from the lake. A single groupBy(seller_id).agg(...) computes all measures; approx_count_distinct is used for distinct buyers to keep it fast. Output written as partitioned Parquet keyed by date.
processingSteps: 1. Read order_lines and project only seller_id, buyer_id, category, amount to shrink the shuffle.
2. groupBy("seller_id") and compute sum, avg, count, approx_count_distinct(buyer_id), and collect_set(category) in one agg() pass.
3. Rely on partial (map-side) aggregation so reducer measures shuffle only small partial states.
4. Alias every measure (total_sales, avg_sale, num_orders, approx_buyers, categories) for a clean schema.
5. Write the per-seller metrics to Parquet partitioned by run date.
endToEndExample.output: A seller_metrics table: seller_id, total_sales, avg_sale, num_orders, approx_buyers, categories (array).
endToEndExample.monitoring: Inspect the Spark UI final aggregate stage for skewed sellers (one heavy task) and for spill from collect_set on sellers with many categories; track output row count equals the number of active sellers.
endToEndExample.errorHandling: Bound collect_set by capping categories (or switch to approx_count_distinct of categories) if a seller has an unexpectedly huge category set; validate that no measure is unexpectedly null.
endToEndExample.finalResult: A fast, stable daily metrics table computed in a single scan and shuffle, where approximate distinct counts keep buyer cardinality cheap and partial aggregation keeps the numeric measures scalable.

industryUseCases.problem: Compute daily plays, average listen time, and distinct listeners per track across tens of billions of stream events.
industryUseCases.solution: groupBy(track_id).agg(sum(play_count), avg(listen_seconds), approx_count_distinct(user_id)) in a single pass.
industryUseCases.benefits: approx_count_distinct makes distinct-listener counts feasible at scale; one agg() pass computes all KPIs efficiently.

industryUseCases.problem: Build per-category sales dashboards with revenue, order counts, and distinct customers refreshed hourly.
industryUseCases.solution: groupBy(category).agg(sum(amount), count('*'), countDistinct(customer_id)) with aliasing, using approx_count_distinct when latency matters.
industryUseCases.benefits: Single-pass, partially-aggregated metrics keep dashboards fresh and cheap to refresh.

industryUseCases.problem: Estimate unique reach (distinct users) per campaign across massive impression logs where exact counts are infeasible.
industryUseCases.solution: approx_count_distinct(user_id) grouped by campaign_id, with tuned rsd to balance accuracy and cost.
industryUseCases.benefits: HyperLogLog sketches deliver bounded-error reach estimates in fixed memory, far cheaper than exact distinct counts.

productionDeepDive.scalability: Reducer aggregates (sum/avg/count/min/max) scale linearly via partial aggregation, shuffling only compact partial states. countDistinct and collectors scale with cardinality/group size; replace them with approx_count_distinct or bounded collection to keep memory flat.
productionDeepDive.faultTolerance: Aggregation recomputes from lineage on task loss; small partial-aggregate shuffles speed recovery, whereas large collect_list shuffles lengthen it. The external shuffle service preserves shuffle files across executor restarts.
productionDeepDive.highAvailability: Aggregations run inside one application; availability depends on the cluster manager and driver. Checkpointing before a heavy aggregate avoids recomputing long lineages after partial failures.
productionDeepDive.disasterRecovery: Aggregation logic is reproducible code; recovery centers on input availability and idempotent output. Partitioned overwrite-by-date writes let a failed metrics job re-run safely.
productionDeepDive.performanceOptimization: Compute all measures in one agg() pass, filter and project before aggregating, use approx_count_distinct for large distinct counts, and avoid unbounded collect_list/collect_set; enable AQE to coalesce post-shuffle partitions.
productionDeepDive.costOptimization: One combined agg() pass instead of many separate scans, plus approximate distinct counts, can cut executor-hours dramatically. Pruning columns before the shuffle reduces serialization and network cost.
productionDeepDive.securityConsiderations: collect_list/collect_set can aggregate raw PII into arrays; hash or mask sensitive columns before collecting, and prefer approx_count_distinct over collect_set+size when you only need cardinality of sensitive fields.
productionDeepDive.monitoringAndObservability: Use the Spark UI to spot skewed groups (a single long final-aggregate task) and disk spill from large collected arrays; emit metrics on output cardinality and on the configured rsd for approximate counts.
productionDeepDive.dataQualityValidation: Validate that count vs count(col) differences match expected null rates, confirm grouped output row counts equal expected group cardinality, and sanity-check approx vs exact counts on a sample to confirm error is within tolerance.
productionDeepDive.loggingAndAlerting: Alert on executor OOM or excessive spill in the aggregate stage (often a runaway collect_list), and log the rsd used for approximate counts so downstream consumers know the accuracy guarantee.

recommendedPractices: **One pass, many measures:** compute all aggregates in a single agg() call.
**Always alias:** name every aggregate column with .alias() for a clean, stable schema.
**Prefer approximate distinct:** use approx_count_distinct on large data when small error is acceptable.
**Bound collectors:** use collect_list/collect_set only when group sizes are known to be small.
engineeringStandards: Filter and select only needed columns before aggregating to minimize shuffle volume.
Document whether each distinct count is exact (countDistinct) or approximate (approx_count_distinct) and its rsd.
Avoid collect_list on unbounded groups; if collection is required, cap or pre-aggregate first.
designRecommendations: Design metric tables so all measures share one groupBy key set and one agg() pass.
Replace collect_set + size() with countDistinct/approx_count_distinct when only the cardinality is needed.
Use conditional aggregation (sum of when()) instead of multiple filtered scans for segmented counts.
namingConventions: Alias measures with descriptive snake_case names (total_amount, unique_customers) rather than auto names like sum(amount).
Prefix approximate measures clearly (approx_buyers) so consumers know they are estimates.
documentationStandards: Record the grain (group key) and the list of measures for each aggregated table.
State the accuracy guarantee (rsd) for any approximate aggregate.
Note null-handling assumptions (e.g. count(*) vs count(col)) for each metric.
testingStrategies: Unit-test aggregates on small fixtures with known totals and distinct counts.
Test that count(*) and count(col) differ exactly by the number of null rows.
Compare approx_count_distinct against exact countDistinct on a sample to confirm the error stays within the configured rsd.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using collect_list on an unbounded or skewed group.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Developers want all values per group and forget the array is held in executor memory.
commonMistakes.impact: Executor OOM or heavy disk spill when a single group has millions of values.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Bound the group, pre-aggregate, or use a scalable aggregate; only collect when group sizes are known to be small.

commonMistakes.mistake: Using exact countDistinct on billions of rows when an estimate would do.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: countDistinct is the obvious function and the cost is not visible until scale.
commonMistakes.impact: Long runtimes, large shuffles, and memory pressure tracking all distinct values.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Use approx_count_distinct with an appropriate rsd; reserve exact counts for cases requiring exactness.

commonMistakes.mistake: Calling agg() multiple times for different measures.
commonMistakes.whyItHappens: Computing metrics incrementally instead of together.
commonMistakes.impact: Multiple scans and shuffles of the same data, wasting compute.
commonMistakes.correctApproach: Pass all aggregate expressions to a single agg() call so Spark computes them in one pass.

comparisonSection.explanation: countDistinct tracks and shuffles every distinct value for an exact result, expensive on high-cardinality data. approx_count_distinct uses fixed-size HLL sketches that merge cheaply, giving a bounded-error estimate (default ~5%, tunable via rsd) at a fraction of the time and memory.

collect_list returns every value (duplicates kept, order non-deterministic); collect_set returns only distinct values. Both build unbounded per-group arrays in memory, so collect_set is preferable when duplicates are not needed, and neither should be used on very large groups.

df.agg(...) with no grouping returns a single summary row over all rows. df.groupBy(key).agg(...) returns one row per group. The same functions and aliasing apply to both; grouping adds a shuffle on the group key.

beginnerQuestions.question: How do you compute the total and average of a column over an entire DataFrame in PySpark?
beginnerQuestions.answer: Call df.agg() with no groupBy: df.agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"), F.avg("amount").alias("avg_amount")). This returns a single row with the total and average.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: Stress that agg() with no grouping produces exactly one summary row, and that .alias() controls the output column names.

beginnerQuestions.question: What is the difference between count("*") and count("column")?
beginnerQuestions.answer: count("*") counts all rows including those with nulls, while count("column") counts only rows where that column is non-null.
beginnerQuestions.explanation: This is a classic trap. Tie it to null handling: most aggregates ignore nulls, so count(col) can be lower than count(*).

intermediateQuestions.question: How do you compute multiple aggregates with custom column names in one pass?
intermediateQuestions.answer: Pass several aggregate expressions to a single agg() call, each with .alias(): df.groupBy("region").agg(F.sum("amount").alias("total"), F.countDistinct("customer_id").alias("uniques")). Spark computes all measures in one scan and shuffle.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Emphasize the efficiency of one pass over multiple agg() calls and the importance of aliasing for downstream usability.

intermediateQuestions.question: What is the difference between collect_list and collect_set, and what is the risk of using them?
intermediateQuestions.answer: collect_list gathers all values per group into an array (duplicates kept, order non-deterministic); collect_set gathers only distinct values. The risk is that both build unbounded arrays in executor memory, so a large group can cause an OOM or heavy spill.
intermediateQuestions.explanation: Mention non-determinism of collect_list order and that collectors should be used only for bounded groups.

advancedQuestions.question: Why is approx_count_distinct so much faster than countDistinct, and what is the trade-off?
advancedQuestions.answer: countDistinct must track every distinct value and shuffle them, so its cost grows with cardinality. approx_count_distinct uses HyperLogLog sketches of fixed size that merge cheaply, so it runs in bounded memory and far faster. The trade-off is a small relative error (default ~5%), tunable via the rsd parameter (lower rsd = more accurate but more memory).
advancedQuestions.explanation: Name HyperLogLog, the fixed-memory sketch idea, and the rsd accuracy knob. Note it ignores nulls like countDistinct.

advancedQuestions.question: Explain partial (map-side) aggregation and why it makes sum/avg/count scalable but not collect_list.
advancedQuestions.answer: Spark computes a partial aggregate on each partition before the shuffle, so for sum/avg/count only small partial states cross the network and merge cheaply. collect_list cannot meaningfully reduce per partition - it must keep every value - so it shuffles and accumulates unbounded data, which is why it scales poorly and risks OOM.
advancedQuestions.explanation: Connect map-side combine to reduced shuffle volume; contrast reducible aggregates with collectors that hold all values.

scenarioBasedQuestions.scenario: Your nightly job computes distinct active users per app over 50 billion events using countDistinct and it keeps spilling and running for hours. How do you fix it?
scenarioBasedQuestions.thinkingProcess: Exact distinct on 50B rows is the bottleneck. If the business tolerates a few percent error, switch to an approximate estimate; otherwise mitigate skew and shuffle.
scenarioBasedQuestions.expectedAnswer: Replace countDistinct(user_id) with approx_count_distinct(user_id), tuning rsd to the accuracy the dashboard tolerates (e.g. 0.02). This uses fixed-memory HLL sketches that merge cheaply, eliminating the heavy shuffle and spill and cutting runtime by orders of magnitude. Validate on a sample that the error is acceptable.

systemDesignQuestions.problemStatement: Design an hourly KPI table (revenue, orders, distinct customers, top categories) per merchant over a high-volume order stream, optimizing for cost and freshness.
systemDesignQuestions.designApproach: Project needed columns, then one groupBy(merchant_id).agg() computing sum(amount), count, approx_count_distinct(customer_id), and a bounded collect_set(category) (or top-N). Alias all measures and write partitioned by hour.
systemDesignQuestions.tradeOffs: Approximate distinct counts trade small error for big cost savings; collect_set risks memory on merchants with many categories, so cap it or use a top-N approach. One agg() pass minimizes scans.
systemDesignQuestions.scalingStrategy: Enable AQE to coalesce/skew-split post-shuffle partitions, tune rsd as volume grows, and replace any unbounded collector with approximate or capped alternatives; partition output by hour for idempotent refreshes.

How would you compute a conditional count (orders over $200) inside agg()?
What does the rsd parameter of approx_count_distinct control?
How does AQE help an aggregation with skewed groups?

cheatSheet.oneLineDefinition: Aggregation reduces rows to summary values via agg() with functions like sum/avg/min/max/count/countDistinct/collect_list/collect_set, over the whole DataFrame or per group, with approx_count_distinct for fast distinct counts.
keyConcepts: agg() works on the whole DataFrame (one row) or on groupBy (one row per group).
Compute many measures in one agg() pass and alias each.
sum/avg/count/min/max use partial (map-side) aggregation and scale well.
countDistinct is exact and costly; approx_count_distinct is HyperLogLog, fast, bounded error.
collect_list keeps duplicates; collect_set keeps distinct; both are unbounded per group.
formulas: approx_count_distinct relative error approximately equals rsd (default rsd ~ 0.05, i.e. ~5%)
interviewPoints: count(*) counts all rows; count(col) ignores nulls.
One agg() call computes many measures in a single pass - always alias.
approx_count_distinct beats countDistinct on large data via HLL sketches.
collect_list/collect_set risk OOM on large groups; collect_list order is non-deterministic.
Partial aggregation makes reducers scale but not collectors.
quickNotes: Whole-DataFrame agg() returns exactly one row.
rsd controls approx_count_distinct accuracy vs memory - smaller is more accurate.
Use collect_set + size() only if you also need the values; else countDistinct.
Filter and select columns before aggregating to shrink the shuffle.

keyTakeaways: agg() applies aggregate functions either to a whole DataFrame (one summary row) or to grouped data (one row per group), and a single call should compute all measures in one pass with .alias() naming each output.

sum, avg, min, max, and count use partial (map-side) aggregation so they shuffle only compact partial states and scale linearly, while collect_list/collect_set and exact countDistinct accumulate unbounded state and can OOM at scale.

approx_count_distinct uses HyperLogLog sketches to estimate cardinality in fixed memory with bounded error (tunable via rsd), making distinct counts feasible on billions of rows where exact countDistinct is too costly.

collect_list keeps all values (duplicates, non-deterministic order) while collect_set keeps only distinct values; use them only on bounded groups and prefer countDistinct when you just need a cardinality.
Know null semantics (count(*) vs count(col)) and combine measures into one agg() pass after filtering and projecting to minimize scans and shuffle volume.
